blocks.text: Composites are very efficient and useful modern materials. A composite is a combination of two or more materials that forms a product with better properties. One component is called the matrix, and the others, which are held in the matrix, are called reinforcement agents; some composites have more than one reinforcement agent. The matrix holds the reinforcement, while the reinforcement provides high strength.

An example is fibreglass, in which a polymer is the matrix and the reinforcement may be fibres of a fabric, glass or carbon-based materials. Composites have a good strength-to-weight ratio and strong resistance to corrosion, so they suit demanding applications: boat hulls and car bodies are made of fibreglass, and carbon fibre is widely used in aircraft and sports gear because it is light and very durable. Fibreglass is also used to insulate walls and ceilings from heat and cold (the book's Figure 31.3 is a photograph of this).

blocks.alt: Left: a rectangular block of yellow matrix with blue fibres running through it; arrows label the matrix (holds the reinforcement) and the fibres (give high strength). Right: fibreglass (polymer matrix and glass fibres) for boat hulls, car bodies and insulation; carbon fibre for aircraft and sports gear; good strength-to-weight ratio and corrosion resistance.
blocks.caption: A composite: matrix and reinforcement (original diagram for topic 31.1.4).
blocks.long_description: The fibres carry the load and make the material strong, while the matrix binds them together, keeps them in place and protects them.

blocks.prompt: Give the roles of the matrix and the reinforcement in a composite.
blocks.explanation: The matrix holds the reinforcement in place; the reinforcement (such as glass or carbon fibres) provides high strength.

items: Fibreglass: boat hulls, car bodies, insulation; carbon fibre: aircraft, sports gear.
